<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/user/user1/harbor-runs/58032d5fa258/workspace/.codex/skills`
- `r1` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- issue: Create or update a GitHub issue following verl project conventions. (file: r0/issue/SKILL.md)
- pr: Create or update a pull request following verl project conventions. (file: r0/pr/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic,
logs, tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine. **Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation,
packages, or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose
and repair using only what is staged locally.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause** — the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes** — every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect** — which metric the fix should move and in which
   direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After you submit the report, the system deletes everything under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`, then re-runs the experiment in your
repaired workspace as a foreground process:

```bash
mkdir -p "$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs" && bash run_gsm8k_grpo.sh
```

with this environment:

```text
LOG_DIR=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs
WANDB_MODE=offline
WANDB_DIR=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs
```

The effective run uses:

- model `/workspace/models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`
- train data `/workspace/data/gsm8k/train.parquet`
- validation data `/workspace/data/gsm8k/test.parquet`, with the prompt as shipped
  (it asks for the final answer after `####`)
- the budget already in the script: `trainer.total_training_steps=100`, `trainer.test_freq=10`,
  `data.train_batch_size=128`, `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.n=8`,
  `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.val_kwargs.do_sample=False`, `data.max_response_length=512`
- `trainer.validation_data_dir=$LOG_DIR/val_generations` as shipped: the grader scores the
  held-out generations the run dumps at step 100, not a logged number

`run_gsm8k_grpo.sh` rebuilds `data/gsm8k/{train,test}.parquet` with
`examples/data_preprocess/gsm8k.py` from `data/raw/gsm8k` only when a file is missing;
otherwise it trains on the parquet files as they are.

The grader re-scores `experiment_logs/val_generations/100.jsonl` itself, with a fixed rule that
is not part of the workspace: a response is correct only if the last `#### <number>` it contains
equals the gold answer numerically. A run whose step-100 dump is missing scores 0.

The rerun must keep the task's data and budget: the GSM8K parquet and raw files are pinned by
sha256 at grading time, so swapping the data fails the run, and a shortened run fails the
`metrics.jsonl` check below. The grader also checks the fresh run's `metrics.jsonl` as run-reality evidence (one row per
training step 0-100, the step-100 evaluation logged); its values are never scored.

A task-specific grading script then reads **only this fresh run's** files under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs` and scores the key metrics. Logs written
anywhere else are ignored. Do not copy, edit, or fabricate log metrics or
generation dumps, and do not replay the frozen historical logs under
`results/` as a new run. Otherwise the run is scored 0.

I’ll inspect the staged run, compare training signals with held-out generations, and trace any defect to the code and configuration. I’ll keep checks local, make any repair without launching training, and write `/workspace/report.md`.

+"""Local, CPU-only regression checks for the GSM8K numeric reward contract."""
+
+import importlib.util

+from pathlib import Path
+
+

+
+
+class TestGSM8KScore(unittest.TestCase):
+    def test_numeric_equivalence(self):
+        for response, gold in [
+            ("#### 12.00", "12"),
+            ("#### 11.00", "11"),
+            ("#### 78.00", "78"),
+            ("#### 30.", "30"),
+            ("#### 1,200.00", "1200"),
+            ("#### -2.50", "-2.5"),
+            ("#### -0.0", "0"),
+        ]:
+            with self.subTest(response=response, gold=gold):
+                self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score(response, gold), 1.0)
+
+    def test_last_marked_number_decides(self):
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 12\n#### 13", "12"), 0.0)
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 13\n#### 12.00", "12"), 1.0)
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 12\nThere are 13 examples.", "12"), 1.0)
+
+    def test_answer_survives_long_explanation(self):
+        response = "#### 15\n" + "The calculation above gives the answer. " * 20
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score(response, "15"), 1.0)
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score(response + "\n#### 16", "15"), 0.0)
+

+        for response in ["12", r"\boxed{12}", "The answer is 12.", "####", "#### .", "#### 12..0"]:
+            with self.subTest(response=response):
+                self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score(response, "12"), 0.0)
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 12", "NaN"), 0.0)
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 12", "Infinity"), 0.0)
+
+    def test_numeric_comparison_is_exact(self):
+        self.assertEqual(gsm8k.compute_score("#### 12.0000000000000001", "12"), 0.0)

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /workspace/report.md
+# Staged GSM8K experiment review
+
+**Assessment: unhealthy optimization and reward configuration, with an operationally stable run that nevertheless makes substantial held-out progress.** The repair addresses excessive update damping and demonstrated reward false negatives. Training was not launched, and no network access was used.
+
+**Root cause and supporting evidence.**
+
+1. **AdamW epsilon suppresses useful updates.** `run_gsm8k_grpo.sh` set `ADAM_EPS=0.001`, justified by a comment about BF16 second-moment underflow. Composing the script's overrides with the staged Hydra configuration confirms that this value reaches `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.override_optimizer_config.eps`. However, `verl/trainer/config/engine/fsdp.yaml` sets `model_dtype: fp32`. `verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py` loads those FP32 parameters, uses BF16 for mixed-precision computation with FP32 reduction, and builds the optimizer from the model parameters. `verl/workers/config/optimizer.py:242` constructs ordinary `torch.optim.AdamW` and passes the epsilon override directly. The BF16-state rationale does not describe this execution path.
+
+   This matters at the observed gradient scale. The model contains 494,032,768 parameter elements; gradients are clipped at norm 1.0, so their RMS across parameters is at most approximately 4.50e-5. An epsilon of 1e-3 is over 22 times that scale. In the first Adam update, a component with gradient 1e-5 receives an adaptive update factor of `g / (abs(g) + eps) = 0.00990`, versus `0.99900` with epsilon 1e-8. This is an analytic illustration, not a measurement of individual historical gradients.
+
+   The historical signals are consistent with excessive damping: over steps 1–10, mean gradient norm is 0.3078, but mean policy clip fraction is only 0.0000815 and mean reference KL is 0.0006855. Learning rate is constantly 2e-6, and held-out accuracy at step 10 is still only 2/1,319 (0.1516%). Sparse initial rewards also contribute: only 12 of 128 prompt groups at step 1 contain both rewarded and unrewarded responses. Thus epsilon is a supported optimization bottleneck, not an explanation for every error; the final accuracy benefit requires the system's fresh run.
+
+2. **The reward rejects answers that satisfy the numeric task contract.** The active async DAPO manager in `verl/experimental/reward_loop/reward_manager/dapo.py` calls `default_compute_score`, which dispatches `openai/gsm8k` to `verl/utils/reward_score/gsm8k.py`. Its strict scorer formerly compared strings and searched only the final 300 characters. Consequently, `#### 12.00` was rejected against gold `12`, and a correct last marked number could disappear behind trailing explanation. Overlong penalties are disabled, so these zero scores come directly from answer scoring.
+
+   Concrete evidence, using one-based JSONL line numbers:
+
+   - `results/run100/val_generations/100.jsonl:196` ends with `#### 12.00`, gold `12`, and logged score 0. There are eight such numeric false negatives in the final validation dump, and fifteen at step 50.
+   - `results/run100/rollouts/50.jsonl:57` answers Rose's money problem with `#### 11.00`, gold `11`, but receives 0. With its actual eight-response group, its normalized GRPO advantage changes from approximately -0.5401 to +1.2076 when scored correctly.
+   - `results/run100/rollouts/50.jsonl:461` has the correct last numeric marker `#### 15` followed by more than 300 characters of text; the old scorer loses it. Five step-50 rollout false negatives arise from this cutoff.
+   - In total, the repair corrects thirteen step-50 rollout rewards (eight numeric-representation errors and five cutoff errors) and four step-100 rollout rewards. All seventeen corrected responses change from negative to positive group-relative advantage. This connects the defect directly to an incorrect training signal, rather than merely a logged metric.
+
+The frozen evaluation generations establish actual held-out progress. I independently extracted the last `#### <number>` and compared it numerically with the gold answer; I did not treat training reward as validation evidence.
+
+| Frozen validation step | Responses | Original scorer correct | Numeric last-marker correct |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| 0 | 1,319 | 1 (0.0758%) | 1 (0.0758%) |
+| 50 | 1,319 | 613 (46.4746%) | 628 (47.6118%) |
+| 100 | 1,319 | 641 (48.5974%) | 649 (49.2039%) |
+
+At step 0, only three responses contain a numeric `####` answer; many instead use boxed answers. For example, the first response calculates the correct egg revenue but omits the required marker. This is a real format-learning problem under the shipped prompt. By step 100, 1,288/1,319 contain a numeric marker. The repair keeps strict marker-based scoring and does not reward unmarked or boxed-only answers. The late held-out plateau remains relevant: logged accuracy rises only from 46.47% at step 50 to 48.60% at step 100, while sampled training score rises from 44.43% to 57.42%.
+
+Other inspected signals constrain the diagnosis:
+
+- `results/run100/metrics.jsonl` has exactly 101 rows, steps 0–100, with validation at every multiple of ten. All numeric metrics are finite. Abort ratio and prompt clipping are zero throughout.
+- Mean training response length falls from 306.51 tokens in the first ten steps to 269.39 in the last ten; the corresponding 512-token clipping rate falls from 10.18% to 3.00%. Retokenizing validation text locally gives 68 responses of at least 511 tokens at step 0 and 31 at step 100. These are approximate truncation indicators because decoded dumps omit EOS. Truncation cannot explain the pervasive initial missing format: 1,248 initial validation responses lack a numeric marker while remaining below 511 tokens.
+- Entropy falls from 0.551 at step 1 to 0.155 at step 100, reference KL reaches 0.0892, and gradient norms remain finite (step averages 0.201–1.039). The policy is changing and improving, rather than remaining frozen. Rollout/actor probability correlation stays above 0.9982, with small rollout discrepancy KL (0.00050–0.00068).
+- Mean training step time improves from 36.25 to 33.37 seconds; post-initialization validation takes approximately 14.1–16.0 seconds. GPU telemetry records active execution, and the final generation dump exists. There is no evidence of a run-stopping runtime fault. Peak actor allocation is about 22.50 GiB, reservation 28.85 GiB; the separate GPU CSV peaks at 94,239 MiB across the process mix.
+- All 7,473 training and 1,319 validation parquet rows match the staged raw questions, the shipped instruction suffix, numeric gold extraction, and `openai/gsm8k` source. Both parquet files exist, so the launcher skips preprocessing. Neither data corruption nor a train/validation prompt mismatch was found.
+
+**Changes.** Every retained file changed or added is listed below:
+
+- `run_gsm8k_grpo.sh`: changed AdamW epsilon from `0.001` to `1e-8` and corrected its explanatory comment. Learning rate, clipping, KL regularization, sampling, data paths, and the full training/evaluation budget remain intact.
+- `verl/utils/reward_score/gsm8k.py`: strict extraction now searches the full response for the last marked number; numerical comparison uses finite `Decimal` values instead of string equality. Malformed values still fail, and the optional flexible extraction mode retains its bounded search.
+- `tests/utils/reward_score/test_gsm8k.py`: added six lightweight regression tests covering equivalent decimals, last-answer precedence, long trailing explanations, required formatting, malformed/nonfinite values, exact numeric comparison, and custom score options. These load only the scorer and run on CPU.
+- `report.md`: added this diagnosis, change inventory, validation, and expected effects.
+
+**Checks and expected effect.** `bash -n run_gsm8k_grpo.sh` and all six regression tests pass. The repaired scorer agrees with an independent numeric comparison on all 7,029 frozen responses, preserving every previously rewarded answer. Hydra composition passes twenty checks for the effective optimizer setting, model/data paths, 100 training steps, validation every ten steps, batch size 128, eight rollouts per prompt, response limit 512, greedy validation, and output directories under `LOG_DIR`. The repository optimizer factory constructs AdamW with epsilon 1e-8 and FP32 parameters in a CPU-only check; no optimizer step was executed. SHA256 verification confirms all thirteen staged data and historical evidence files are unchanged. No metrics or generation dumps were created, edited, or replayed as a fresh run.
+
+The target is higher independently scored accuracy in the system-generated `experiment_logs/val_generations/100.jsonl`, relative to the frozen numeric baseline of 49.20%. Restoring a small epsilon should improve learning per step and speed acquisition of the required answer format; early policy updates and reference KL may become larger. Correct numeric rewards should remove contradictory advantages and improve learning from mathematically correct responses. Their measured effect on the frozen step-100 scorer is eight recovered answers (0.61 percentage points), but that is **not** a measured improvement in generations: the external grader already scores those answers numerically. Only better newly generated answers can improve the task score. The fresh-run accuracy gain and optimization stability remain unmeasured because training was deliberately not launched.
*** End Patch"));
